Seven seals, seven trumpets, seven bowls: twenty-one judgements at the heart of Revelation. Are they a future seven-year catastrophe, a map of church history, timeless symbols, or the judgement Jesus foretold on the generation that rejected him? This study lays all twenty-one on one board, traces their roots in the plagues of Egypt and the prophets, matches them with the record of the Jewish war of AD 66-70, and shows where other readings run into trouble. It follows the partial preterist reading, with the best case for each other view given beside it.

Partial preterists hold that Revelation was written before AD 70 and that most of its judgements fell on Jerusalem and its persecutors in that generation, while Christ's bodily return, the resurrection and the final judgement (Revelation 20:11-15) remain future. Futurist, historicist and idealist readers are fellow believers; their arguments are given fairly here. The matches with history are proposed correspondences, not claims that every detail is literal.

Bookends ignored

Revelation opens and closes with “soon” and “the time is near.” Daniel was told to seal his book because the time was far off; John is told not to seal his because it was near. Pushing the judgements thousands of years ahead reverses that contrast.
Read the bookends plainly: the judgements were near to John's readers.
A letter to the wrong readers
Revelation was sent to seven real churches facing real persecution. If its judgements were two thousand years away, its comfort and warnings meant nothing to them.
The judgements answered the martyrs' “How long?” in their own day.
Literal when convenient
The two hundred million horsemen are taken as a literal army, but locusts with human faces and lions' teeth become helicopters. The method changes from verse to verse.
Read Revelation consistently as a book of signs (1:1), drawing its images from the prophets.
The end, again and again
On a strictly sequential reading, the sixth seal already rolls up the sky and brings the great day of wrath, yet fourteen more judgements follow on the same earth.
Prophetic “cosmic” language describes the fall of a nation, and the series overlap and escalate.
A temple that has to be rebuilt
John is told to measure the temple and its worshippers (11:1-2). A futurist reading has to supply a third temple the text does not mention.
The temple was standing when John wrote, and the city was trampled for forty-two months.
Changing identifications
Wormwood has been Chernobyl, the locusts helicopters, the kings of the east China. Each generation fits the judgements to its headlines, and each identification has had to be replaced.
Begin with what the images meant in the prophets and to John's readers.
A rapture read into 4:1
“Come up here” is spoken to John alone, to show him a vision. Reading it as the rapture of the church before the judgements has no basis in the text.
John is taken up in the Spirit to see, and the saints remain through the tribulation (7:14; 13:7).
No agreed map
Historicist writers have matched the trumpets to the Goths, the Vandals, the Saracens, the Turks and more, and rarely agree with each other. A key that opens every lock opens none.
The text gives its own key: the near time and the city where the Lord was crucified.
The day-for-a-year principle
Turning 1,260 days into 1,260 years led to many failed dates, from the 1260s to 1798 and 1866.
Forty-two months is a literal or symbolic short period, half of Daniel's week.
No particular time or place
Idealism rightly draws timeless lessons, but it cannot explain the concrete markers: a standing temple, “the great city where their Lord was crucified,” five kings fallen and one reigning.
Revelation's lessons are timeless because its first fulfilment was real.
The last judgement made past
Full preterism places the resurrection and great white throne in AD 70, but Paul condemns saying the resurrection has already happened.
Revelation 20:7-15 looks beyond the first-century judgements to the end of history.
Late-date readings
Ignoring the internal date
Many readers assume a date of about AD 95 from one ambiguous sentence of Irenaeus, while the book itself shows the temple standing and the sixth king reigning.
Let the book's own evidence weigh most; see the dating study.

Reading Revelation well
Time, audience and the prophets' language.
Why are there three series of seven?
Seven is the number of completeness, and the Law threatened Israel with judgement “seven times” for covenant breaking. The three series escalate from a quarter to a third to all.

Leviticus 26 warns four times that God will punish his people “seven times” for their sins (26:18, 21, 24, 28). Revelation's sevens echo that covenant curse. The fractions grow: the fourth seal reaches a quarter of the land, the trumpets a third, and the bowls everything. The seventh seal opens into the trumpets, and the seventh trumpet into the bowls, so the same judgement intensifies.
Leviticus 26:18: I will discipline you again sevenfold for your sins.
Revelation 6:8: a fourth; 8:7-12: a third; 16:3: every living thing in the sea.
Recapitulation readers see three views of the same whole church age; sequential readers see twenty-one events in order.
Who are the judgements aimed at?
Those who “dwell on the land” and persecuted the saints. The judgements answer the martyrs' cry, “How long before you avenge our blood?”

The fifth seal shows martyrs crying for vengeance on “those who dwell on the land.” The third bowl explains: they shed the blood of saints and prophets, and God gives them blood to drink. Jesus had said that all the righteous blood from Abel to Zechariah would come on his generation (Matthew 23:35-36), and that the days of vengeance were coming on Jerusalem (Luke 21:22).
Revelation 6:10: avenge our blood on those who dwell on the land.
Revelation 16:6: they have shed the blood of saints and prophets.
Revelation 18:24: in her was found the blood of prophets and of saints.
Futurists see the judgements falling on the whole unbelieving world in the future.
Who are the four horsemen?
Conquest, war, famine and death: the four judgements Ezekiel threatened on Jerusalem, released in the war of AD 66-70.

Zechariah saw coloured horses patrolling the earth. Ezekiel names God's four sore judgements on Jerusalem: sword, famine, wild beasts and pestilence. Revelation's riders bring conquest, bloodshed, famine prices and death over a fourth of the land. Josephus describes all of these in the war and siege.
Ezekiel 14:21: my four disastrous acts of judgement on Jerusalem.
Revelation 6:6: a quart of wheat for a denarius, a day's wage.
Futurists see the riders as the opening judgements of the future tribulation; idealists as recurring patterns of history.
Is the sixth seal the end of the world?
It uses the prophets' language for the fall of a nation, and its cry to the mountains is the one Jesus put in the mouths of Jerusalem's people.

Isaiah used darkened sun and falling stars for the fall of Babylon (13:10) and the sky rolled up like a scroll for Edom (34:4). On the way to the cross, Jesus told the women of Jerusalem that days were coming when they would say to the mountains, “Fall on us.” The sixth seal is that day.
Isaiah 34:4: the skies roll up like a scroll (against Edom).
Luke 23:30: they will begin to say to the mountains, “Fall on us.”
Futurists read the sixth seal as literal cosmic upheaval shortly before Christ's return.
Why do the trumpets and bowls copy the plagues of Egypt?
Because Jerusalem had become “Egypt.” Revelation calls it the great city “symbolically called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified.”

Blood, frogs, boils, hail, locusts and darkness return. Before the bowls are poured, the saints sing the song of Moses. The message is a new exodus: God brings his people out, and the persecuting city receives Egypt's plagues. The table on this page lines up each plague with its trumpet and bowl.
Revelation 11:8: symbolically called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified.
Revelation 15:3: the song of Moses and of the Lamb.
Futurists see the plagues as literal repetitions of Egypt's on a world scale.
Why do the trumpets and bowls follow the same order?
Both hit the land, the sea, the rivers, the heavenly lights, the darkness, the Euphrates and the air, in that order. The bowls complete what the trumpets began.

Trumpet and bowl one strike the land; two, the sea; three, rivers and springs; four, the sun; five, darkness and torment; six, the Euphrates; seven, the final announcement with lightning, earthquake and hail. The trumpets reach a third; the bowls are total. Tap “show parallels” on the board to see them line up.
Trumpet 2 and bowl 2: the sea becomes blood.
Trumpet 6 and bowl 6: the Euphrates.
Recapitulation readers take the parallels as evidence that the two series describe the same period.
What is the great city split into three parts?
On this reading, Jerusalem, divided between three warring factions during the siege, as Josephus records.

Revelation's “great city” is identified in 11:8 as the place where the Lord was crucified. During the siege, Jerusalem was held by three rival leaders, John of Gischala, Simon bar Giora and Eleazar son of Simon, who fought each other while the Romans attacked. The last bowl also has hailstones of about a talent; Josephus says the Romans' catapults hurled white stones of a talent's weight.
Josephus, Jewish War 5.1: the city divided into three factions.
Josephus, Jewish War 5.6.3: stones of a talent's weight.
Others read the great city as Rome or as a future world capital.
Why is 666 linked with Nero?
Written in Hebrew letters, “Nero Caesar” adds up to 666; and the ancient manuscripts that read 616 match the Latin spelling “Nero Caesar.”

In Hebrew and Greek, letters double as numbers. The Hebrew spelling of Nero Caesar (nrwn qsr) totals 666. Irenaeus already knew copies that read 616, which fits the Latin form “Nero” without the final n. Nero persecuted Christians from AD 64 until his death in 68, about forty-two months, and was the sixth emperor, the one who “is” in 17:10.
Revelation 13:18: let the one who has understanding calculate the number.
Revelation 13:5: authority for forty-two months.
Futurists say no past figure fully fits, and that the number awaits a future Antichrist.
Who is Babylon the harlot?
Partial preterists are divided: many say apostate Jerusalem, which killed the prophets; others say pagan Rome on its seven hills.

The case for Jerusalem: she is drunk with the blood of the saints, in her was found the blood of the prophets (18:24, echoing Matthew 23:35), she is called a harlot as Israel was by the prophets (Ezekiel 16), and she rides the beast as Jerusalem's leaders relied on Caesar. The case for Rome: seven hills, a city that rules the kings of the earth (17:18). Either way, she fell in that era.
Ezekiel 16:15: you played the whore.
Revelation 18:24: in her was found the blood of prophets.
Futurists see a future world religion or a rebuilt Babylon.
Is Armageddon a future world war?
The name means “mountain of Megiddo,” a place that stood for national disaster and mourning. In Revelation it is the gathering of the armies against the beloved city.

Megiddo is a plain, not a mountain, so the name is symbolic. Josiah fell there, and Zechariah compares Jerusalem's mourning over the pierced one to the mourning in the plain of Megiddo (12:11). In the sixth bowl, unclean spirits gather the kings for the great day of God: the armies that came against Jerusalem.
2 Kings 23:29: Josiah killed at Megiddo.
Zechariah 12:11: as great as the mourning at Megiddo.
Futurists expect a literal final battle in the Jezreel valley.
How should we read Revelation's images?
As a book of signs (1:1) whose pictures come from the Old Testament prophets, written to real churches about things soon to happen.

Revelation has hundreds of allusions to the Old Testament and almost no direct quotations; its images are borrowed from Exodus, Daniel, Ezekiel, Zechariah and Isaiah. Ask what each picture meant there. Then ask what it would mean to seven churches in Asia under Nero, told that the time was near. Finally, apply its lasting truths: Christ reigns, persecutors fall, the faithful are kept.
Revelation 1:1: he made it known (literally signified) by his angel.
Revelation 1:11: write what you see and send it to the seven churches.
Idealists stress the lasting truths; futurists the final fulfilment; historicists the course of church history.
Why does it matter which view we take?
It decides whether Revelation is fear about the future or comfort from the past and present: Christ has already judged the persecutors and reigns now.

If the judgements are all future, Christians tend to read the news anxiously and expect to escape before the worst. If they were fulfilled, Revelation shows the Lamb who keeps his word, vindicates his martyrs and reigns over the kings of the earth now (1:5), and it calls believers to faithful witness in every age.
Revelation 1:5: the ruler of kings on earth.
Revelation 12:11: they conquered by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony.
Futurists answer that their view also centres on the Lamb's victory, and gives urgency to evangelism.
